demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened
I remind myself it could have been worse
try hard not think about the trauma

Memory.value: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
I should have protected others and I failed

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Water/Flooding): Water, flooding, or large bodies of water
issues.explanation: Water/flooding triggers are hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of accidentally causing serious injury to another in a car accident, given the rest of the profile centers on crash-related and guilt/shame themes. This trigger introduces a different threat context without support from memory or appraisal items.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Feelings: Allowing myself to feel any strong emotion
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Feelings' is internally incoherent as worded: 'Allowing myself to feel any strong emotion' describes the opposite of avoidance. Within the maladaptive strategies node, it directly conflicts with an avoidance strategy.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body
issues.explanation: 'Body Unreliable' fits poorly with the rest of the profile for a perpetration-type accident trauma in which the patient's appraisals otherwise center on guilt, humiliation, and shattered beliefs. There are no memory, trigger, or strategy items suggesting bodily injury, panic/somatic threat, or physical incapacity to support this appraisal.

vignette:
Clinical Vignette: Rajesh Patel

Rajesh Patel was forty-two when the accident happened, a meticulous tax inspector with fifteen years of clean driving and a reputation for caution. On a Tuesday afternoon in March, he had left his office early to pick up his daughter from school. The intersection near Maple and Fifth was one he knew well-he had driven through it hundreds of times. But that day, a delivery truck ran the red light while Rajesh was crossing, and his sedan was struck broadside. The impact was violent and immediate. He heard the shriek of metal tearing, the explosive pop of the airbag, and beneath it all, a sound he would never quite forget: the cry of the other driver, a young woman in the truck, screaming as she realized what she had done. The paramedics arrived within minutes. Rajesh walked away with a fractured collarbone and bruised ribs. The young woman-Sarah, he learned later-suffered a severe head injury, a fractured femur, and spent six weeks in intensive care. She survived, but the trajectory of her life had been altered in that moment, and Rajesh carried the knowledge that his vehicle, his body, his presence at that intersection had been the instrument of her suffering.

In the months that followed, Rajesh developed an elaborate system of self-punishment. He had come to believe that he deserved to suffer because of what had happened, even though the police report had clearly stated that the truck driver bore responsibility. When intrusive images of the crash surfaced-the moment of impact, Sarah's face in the ambulance-he would deliberately remind himself that it could have been worse, that at least she was alive, that he had no right to feel relief about anything. He had failed to protect her, he told himself, though she was a stranger. He should have anticipated the truck, should have driven more defensively, should have taken a different route. These thoughts formed a relentless commentary on his character. Rajesh was certain that he was fundamentally damaged, that the world was not the safe, predictable place he had once believed it to be, and that his survival while Sarah suffered proved something shameful about him.

Whenever Rajesh encountered a trigger-a car accident on the news, a funeral announcement in the office, or worse, someone asking him casually how he was doing after the accident-his maladaptive strategies would activate almost automatically. A colleague mentioning a car crash on the highway sent Rajesh spiraling into thought suppression, trying desperately not to think about the trauma, but the effort itself became exhausting and paradoxically amplified the very thoughts he was fighting. When he saw a hearse pass his office window one afternoon, he gripped the edge of his desk and began the downward comparison ritual again: at least she didn't die, at least he wasn't paralyzed, at least his family wasn't destroyed. Yet these reassurances only deepened his sense of humiliation-the fact that he needed to console himself this way felt like further evidence of his moral failure. The punishment thinking would intensify, and he would find himself cataloguing all the ways he deserved to suffer.

His memories of the event remained fragmented and disturbingly vivid in places. When he tried to recall the sequence of what happened, whole seconds seemed to have vanished. He could remember the sound of Sarah's scream with perfect clarity-it played back in his head whenever he closed his eyes-but the moment just before impact was completely blank, a missing piece. Some moments were frozen in crystalline detail: the way the afternoon light caught the windshield, the exact angle of the truck's hood as it struck his car. Other moments were entirely gone. This incomplete picture haunted him because it meant his mind was unreliable, that he could not fully account for what he had done, and that incompleteness fed directly back into his conviction that he had failed in some crucial way. The fragmented memories seemed to confirm that something was broken inside him, that his perception of reality itself had shattered along with the car's frame. And when memories surfaced unbidden-triggered by a conversation about the accident, or the sight of a damaged vehicle on the street-the vividness of what he could remember, combined with the terrifying gaps, would send him back into his maladaptive cycles, trying to suppress the thoughts, punishing himself for surviving, comparing downward to avoid the full weight of his guilt.

Rajesh's marriage had become strained. His wife, Priya, had initially been supportive, but his withdrawal and self-recrimination had worn on her. He could not accept her reassurances. When she tried to remind him that he was not responsible for the truck driver's error, he would turn away, convinced that she did not understand the depth of his culpability. At work, he had begun to avoid certain routes to the office, taking a longer drive each morning to stay away from the intersection where it had happened. But avoidance had its own cost: he was arriving late more often, and his manager had begun to notice. The meticulous, reliable Rajesh seemed distracted, sometimes appearing to freeze at his desk for no apparent reason. He had not attended his cousin's funeral six months after the accident, making an excuse about work, unable to face the sight of grief made visible. Now, a year and a half later, Rajesh had come to therapy not because he believed he deserved help, but because Priya had insisted, and because the thought suppression and punishment cycles had become so consuming that he could barely function. What frightened him most was the possibility that his suffering would never be enough to balance what Sarah had endured, and that no amount of self-condemnation would ever restore the world to the way it had been before he drove through that intersection.
